blocks.title: Honors — a diagram is an argument
blocks.markdown: A free-body diagram isn't decoration — it's a claim about *which* forces are real and *why*. CPA draws the arrows correctly. Honors has to **justify every arrow on the page**: name the source of each force, and name what you assumed away by leaving other things off.

## Justify each force you draw

For every arrow on your free-body diagram, you should be able to answer two questions:

1. **What object is pushing or pulling here?** Every force has a source. Weight comes from Earth's gravity. The normal force comes from the surface. Tension comes from the string. Friction comes from the surface resisting sliding. If you can't name the *other object* exerting it, the arrow doesn't belong.
2. **Is this force acting on *my* object?** The FBD shows only the forces *on* the body — never the forces the body exerts on other things (those live on *their* diagrams).

An arrow you can't source is a guess. A missing arrow is a force you forgot. Both are arguments you'd lose.

blocks.title: State your assumptions
blocks.markdown:
Every clean free-body diagram is built on idealizations you should say out loud:

- **Massless string** — so tension is the same all along it, and the string adds no weight of its own.
- **Frictionless surface** — drawn only when you've *decided* friction is small enough to ignore (a modeling choice, not a fact).
- **Point particle** — the object is treated as a dot with all forces acting at one point, so you can ignore rotation and how the object is shaped.

These assumptions make the diagram solvable. They also make it *wrong* in situations where they don't hold. An honors FBD names them; it doesn't smuggle them in.

blocks.frame: On my free-body diagram I drew the forces ___. Each one is justified because its source is ___. I left off ___ because I assumed ___, which is safe here since ___.
blocks.prompt: JUSTIFY (homework): Draw the free-body diagram for one scenario from today (a box on an incline, a hanging sign, a cart pulled by a string). Then write a paragraph defending it: name the *source* of every arrow you drew, and name every idealization you assumed (massless string, frictionless, point particle) and why each is reasonable here.
